To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of E. coli (fecal indicator bacteria) in drinking water is weakly associated with diarrheal disease in Cambodia.

E. coli counts of 11-1,000/100 ml in household drinking water were positively associated with increased diarrheal disease and dysentery risks in rural Cambodia, but that the magnitude of the risk was not greater for higher E. coli counts.
(1) E. coli in water is associated with diarrheal disease and (2) this association is weak and not dose-dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between E.coli in household drinking water (a bacterial indicator) and diarrheal risks in rural households in Cambodia.
the extent to which E. coli in water can be used to predict risks from other classes of pathogens.
the relationship between E. coli levels in household drinking water in a tropical setting and the incidence of diarrheal diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of E. coli is associated with diarrheal disease, but the strength and nature of the association are not yet clear.
the association between E.coli counts in drinking water and diarrhoeal diseases was not strong, and that the relationship is likely to depend on the type of pathogen causing the diarrhoeal diseases.
E. coli counts may be a useful indicator for the risk of diarrheal disease in Cambodia but the association between E.coli counts and diarrheal risks is weak.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of diarrheal disease was not increased in households with low concentrations of E. coli and that risk increased only slightly in households with high concentrations of E. colia.
the association between E.coli in household drinking water is not a strong one, but it is positive and statistically significant.

the risk of diarrhea was weakly and non-linearly related to E. coli in the drinking water, with a possible threshold at 100 E. coli/ 100 ml, and that the risks of diarrhea with blood were weakly and linearly related to E coli in the drinking-water.
The main takeaway from our work is that
E. coli counts do not reliably predict risks of diarrheal diseases from all classes of pathogen.
E. coli in water is not a reliable indicator of diarrheal risk in Cambodia, and may be an unreliable indicator in other tropical settings.
E. coli in the drinking water of households in this rural Cambodian village did not reliably indicate the risk of diarrheal disease.
